Simone, the draft came back from the other side last night and I want you to know what you are walking into before Wednesday. There are forty redlines in the document, and thirty-five of them are boilerplate. Do not spend one minute on those. Five of them matter. The real sticking point is the liability cap. They want it at one times the annual fee, and our client cannot live with that. Here is how I would like you to handle it. Do not say no. Say we would be prepared to move on the cap if they accepted a carve-out for fraud, and see what comes back. If they refuse everything, our fallback is a side letter that covers the same ground without touching the main document, but do not put that on the table on Wednesday. And please remember to write subject to contract at the top of every email you send them this week. Nothing you write is binding until the contract is signed, and I want that in black and white. If the tone turns hard, stay in good faith and keep the door open. Nobody is going to walk away over a carve-out.

It is Tuesday night and I am building the script for tomorrow. Forty redlines, and I have already put thirty-five of them in the boilerplate pile. I accept those without a word, because arguing about a standard clause is how a round dies of old age. The five that are left go on one page, and at the top of that page, in capital letters, is the sticking point: the liability cap. My rule for tomorrow is that I never open my mouth with the word no. Every answer starts with would. We would be prepared to move on the cap if you accepted a carve-out for fraud. Would you be willing to look at a longer notice period instead? It costs me nothing, it concedes nothing, and it tells them exactly what trade I am looking for. If they close the door on all five, I have a fallback in my folder, a short side letter that covers the same ground outside the main document, and I am not showing it tomorrow. Every email goes out marked subject to contract, so nothing I write this week binds my client. And whatever the tone becomes at eleven o'clock, I stay in good faith, because nobody should have to walk away from a good deal over one carve-out.

First, the draft comes back from the other side and you read every redline in the document. Then, you separate the boilerplate, which you accept without arguing, from the five changes that really matter to your client. After that, you name the sticking point out loud, because a round that never names it goes in circles for weeks. Next, you make a softened offer instead of a refusal: we would be prepared to move on the cap if you accepted a carve-out for fraud. Finally, if the other side refuses everything, you take out your fallback, you keep the conversation in good faith, and you never walk away in the same meeting.
